statement: The historical and modern definitions differ. In XVI, manuscript pp.~1--3, Loc~(1) requires isomorphisms, two out of three, and the implication \[ gf,fg\in\W\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f,g\in\W \] for $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to X$. Loc~(1 bis) adds closure under retracts in the arrow category. Loc~(1 ter) says that $f\in\W$ whenever its image in $\Cat[\W^{-1}]$ is invertible. Loc~(2) concerns categories with a terminal object. The literal Loc~(3) is the absolute Theorem~A statement: $u:A\to B$ belongs to $\W$ if every $A/b$ is $\W$-aspherical. The relative Theorem~A in our conventions is printed as Loc~(3 bis), not Loc~(3) \citep[ms.~1--3]{AGGrothendieckXVI}.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 1–3; Loc (1), (1 bis), (1 ter), (2), (3), (3 bis), footnote 1
notes: Relative Theorem A is printed 3 bis. Modern strong saturation is not assumed for every historical weak localizer; the historical minimum is nevertheless W_infinity by A.19.

statement: The exact two excision axioms of XII. Let $X$ be a small category, $U,V\subseteq X$ full sieves, $U\cup V=X$, and $S=U\cap V$. Every arrow of $X$ lies in $U$ or $V$, so the square \[ \begin{tikzcd} S\ar[r,"i_1"]\ar[d,"i_2"']&U\ar[d,"j_2"]\\ V\ar[r,"j_1"']&X \end{tikzcd} \tag{A.MV} \] is a pushout and a pullback in $\Cat$. XII, manuscript pp.~75--76, calls W(7 bis) the assertion \[ i_1\in\W\ \Longleftrightarrow\ j_1\in\W, \qquad i_2\in\W\ \Longleftrightarrow\ j_2\in\W. \] The second equivalence follows from the first by exchanging $U$ and $V$. W(7), manuscript pp.~76--77, concerns a strict natural transformation $f:X_\bullet\to Y_\bullet$ between two such squares. With $0$ the intersection, $1,2$ the pieces, and $3$ the union, it says that any two of \[ f_0\in\W,\qquad (f_1,f_2\in\W),\qquad f_3\in\W \] imply the third. These are quantifications over all small categories and all such maps of covers, including empty intersections and empty pieces \citep[ms.~75--77]{AGGrothendieckXII}.
notes: Exact all-small-category and strict map-of-MV-covers quantifiers, with empty pieces and intersections included.

statement: Loc~(6), its three cube clauses, and Loc~(6$'$). XVI, manuscript pp.~16$'$--18$'$, uses the same map $f:X_\bullet\to Y_\bullet$ of MV squares and defines \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \mathrm{Loc}(6a)&:& f_0,f_1,f_2\in\W\ \Longrightarrow\ f_3\in\W,\\ \mathrm{Loc}(6b)&:& f_1,f_2,f_3\in\W\ \Longrightarrow\ f_0\in\W,\\ \mathrm{Loc}(6c)&:& f_0,f_3\in\W\ \Longrightarrow\ f_1,f_2\in\W. \end{array} \] After footnote~13, Loc~(6) means $(6a)+(6b)$, expressly excluding $(6c)$. On the single square (A.MV), Loc~$(6'a)$ is $i_1\in\W\Rightarrow j_1\in\W$, and Loc~$(6'b)$ is $j_1\in\W\Rightarrow i_1\in\W$. Thus XII W(7 bis) is XVI Loc~$(6')$, whereas XII W(7) includes all three clauses $(6a,b,c)$.
notes: XII W(7) includes all three cube clauses; XVI Loc (6) excludes 6c after footnote 13.

statement: Cofibrations and the four structural formulations. For a functor $i:A\to B$, let \[ i_!:A\backslash\Cat\longrightarrow B\backslash\Cat, \qquad (A\to X)\longmapsto(B\to B\amalg_A X). \] The class $\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$ consists of the $i$ for which $i_!$ sends every morphism whose underlying functor is in $\W$ to another such morphism. XVI, manuscript pp.~25--27, states: \[ \begin{array}{p{20mm}p{112mm}} Loc~$(6A)$&Every $f:A\to B$ factors in $\Cat$ as $A\xrightarrow{i}M\xrightarrow{p}B$, with $i\in\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$ and $p\in\W$.\\[3pt] Loc~$(6A')$&Every Dwyer map belongs to $\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$.\\[3pt] Loc~$(6B)$&Every MV square (A.MV) is $\W$-homotopy cocartesian.\\[3pt] Loc~$(6C)$&In every $\W$-homotopy cocartesian square (A.MV), now without any sieve or strict-pushout hypothesis, $j_1\in\W$ implies $i_1\in\W$. \end{array} \] Here $\W$-homotopy cocartesian means that the canonical comparison from a specified Grothendieck model of the homotopy pushout to the fourth vertex belongs to $\W$. Under enough cofibrations this agrees with the cofibration-replacement definition of XII, manuscript pp.~261--264.
notes: Intrinsic preservation definition; Dwyer means classical full sieve with right adjoint on generated cosieve; no false closure under retracts is used.

statement: Strict fibrations and the auxiliary classes. For $p:E\to S$, the class $\Fib_{\W}$ is defined by strict base change: \[ p\in\Fib_{\W}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \bigl(u:X\to Y\text{ over }S,\ u\in\W\bigr) \Rightarrow\bigl(E\times_S X\to E\times_S Y\bigr)\in\W. \] We write $\W_S^u$ for morphisms over $S$ whose pullbacks along every $S'\to S$ lie in $\W$. A functor $E\to S$ itself lies in $\W^u$ when all its strict base changes lie in $\W$. The class $\mathcal F_{\W}$ consists of Grothendieck fibrations $p:E\to S$ whose reindexing functors $\alpha^*:E_t\to E_s$, for every $\alpha:s\to t$ in $S$, lie in $\W$. XVI, manuscript pp.~27--32, calls $p$ weakly $\W$-fibrant if, for every $T'\to T$ over $S$ with $T,T'$ contractible in the category-homotopy sense, $E\times_S T'\to E\times_S T$ is in $\W$. This defines $\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W}$. Finally, $\Parf_{\W}$ means both $\W$-smooth and $\W$-proper. The manuscript has \[ \Parf_{\W}\subseteq\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W},\quad \mathcal F_{\W}\subseteq\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W},\quad \Fib_{\W}\subseteq\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_{\W}. \] These are different classes; a Grothendieck fibration is not, by definition, a member of $\Fib_{\W}$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 27–32; intrinsic, Grothendieck, weak and perfect fibrations
notes: Strict base change is distinguished from homotopy pullback and from Grothendieck fibration; variance of reindexing maps is explicit.

statement: The exact fibration axioms. XVI, manuscript pp.~38--45, defines Loc~(7) to mean Loc~$(7a)$: \[ \mathrm{Loc}(7a):\quad \mathcal F_{\W}\subseteq\Fib_{\W}. \] Loc~$(7b)$ says that, whenever $p:X\to S$ and $q:Y\to S$ belong to $\mathcal F_{\W}$, a functor $f:X\to Y$ over $S$ with $f\in\W$ lies in $\W_S^u$. Equivalently in this situation, every strict fibre map $f_s:X_s\to Y_s$ lies in $\W$. Loc~$(7c)$ says \[ \mathcal F_{\W}\cap\W\subseteq\W^u. \] For a reference localizer $V\subseteq\W$, Loc~$(7D_V)$ is \[ \Parf_V\cap\W\subseteq\W^u. \] Loc~$(7D)$ without a subscript means $V=\W$. The weakest reference version singled out by the manuscript is $D_{W_\omega}$, with its historical minimum $W_\omega$; the modern version used in this paper is $D_{\Winfty}$. Loc~$(7F)$ means that every functor $f:X\to Y$ admits a factorization \[ X\xrightarrow{u}E\xrightarrow{p}Y, \qquad u\in\W,\quad p\in\Fib_{\W}. \] For fundamental localizers, all $X\to e$ belong to $\Fib_{\W}$, by product stability. Thus the associated category of fibrant objects has all objects fibrant. The word ``cofibrations'' in the initial formulation of $(7F)$ on manuscript p.~39 is a variance error; the subsequent formulations explicitly say fibrations.
notes: The word cofibrations in the first 7F wording is a variance error; reference D_V and absolute D_W are separated.

statement: The four other numbered conditions used in the audit. Loc~(4), XVI manuscript p.~8, is \[ \coprod_{i\in I}u_i\in\W\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_i\in\W\text{ for every }i\in I \] for every small family, including $I=\varnothing$. Loc~(5), manuscript p.~12, is $\W\subseteq\W_0$, where $\W_0$ consists of functors inducing bijections on connected components. Loc~(8), manuscript pp.~71--72, is closure of $\W$ under all small filtered colimits in the arrow category of $\Cat$; Loc~(8 bis) asks only for sequential colimits. Loc~(9), manuscript pp.~74--75, says that $\W$ is an accessible full subcategory of the arrow category, with its inclusion accessible. It does not mean preservation of every filtered colimit.
notes: All filtered colimits is stronger than accessibility. The source uses a countable-cardinality convention distinct from modern finite accessibility.

statement: Brown's lemma in the form needed in XVI 3.2.1. Let $\mathcal M$ have an initial object $0$ and let $C,\W\subseteq\Fl(\mathcal M)$. Assume that $\W$ contains identities and satisfies two out of three; $C$ contains isomorphisms and all $0\to X$, is closed under composition and pushout, and all pushouts along maps in $C$ exist; every map factors as a map in $C$ followed by a map in $\W$; and pushouts of maps in $C\cap\W$ belong to $C\cap\W$. Then $C\subseteq\operatorname{Cof}_{\W}$. Neither strong saturation nor closure of $C$ under retracts is needed.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Lemma 3.2.1, ms. 20–22; XII footnote 136, ms. 266
notes: Complete typed relative Brown argument supplied; no retract closure of the cofibration class or strong saturation is needed.

statement: The consequences of enough cofibrations and their duals. Let $\W$ contain identities and satisfy two out of three. Suppose pushouts exist and every morphism of $\mathcal M$ factors as a $\W$-cofibration followed by a $\W$-equivalence. Then \[ \operatorname{Cof}_{\W}\cap\W =\{i:\text{every pushout of }i\text{ belongs to }\W\}. \] Moreover, a $\W$-equivalence between objects cofibrant under a fixed $A$ stays in $\W$ after arbitrary cobase change $A\to A'$. Dually, enough $\W$-fibrations implies that a $\W$-equivalence between objects fibrant over $S$ lies in $\W_S^u$, and $\Fib_{\W}\cap\W=\W^u$.
notes: No implicit retract closure or abstract model-category lifting axiom. Exact assumptions are existence of pushouts, identities and two out of three, and intrinsic cofibration factorizations.

statement: The elementary implications between the excision clauses. Using only two out of three and the definitions of MV squares, one has \[ (6a)\Rightarrow(6'a),\qquad (6b)\Rightarrow(6'b),\qquad (6c)\Rightarrow(6'a)+(6'b). \] Consequently XII W(7) implies W(7 bis), as Proposition~6 at manuscript p.~78 correctly states.
notes: Two specified degenerate cubes prove the arrows; repeated source label f_1=j_1 is corrected to f_2=j_1.

statement: The missing cofibration premise and its repair. For the modern fundamental-localizer convention, Loc~$(6a)$, $(6'a)$, $(6A)$, $(6A')$, and $(6B)$ all hold. The equivalences asserted in XVI Proposition~3.6 and its footnote~19 are therefore valid in this convention. The proof gap identified in XII footnote~136 is real in the argument as originally written: termwise replacement by maps in $\W$ does not by itself show that ordinary pushout preserves them. The Dwyer pushout comparison and the gluing proof in Part~B provide that missing premise without reverse excision.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Proposition 3.6, ms. 25–26, footnote 19; XII ms. 266, footnote 136
notes: Automatic for modern fundamental localizers, without reverse excision. Actual endpoint-product cylinder is used, not pushout-product.

statement: The reversible equivalences and the role of retracts. For a modern fundamental localizer the following are equivalent: \[ \mathrm{Loc}(6b),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6'b),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6C), \quad\mathrm{Loc}(6),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6'),\quad\mathrm{Loc}(6c), \quad\mathrm{W}(7). \] In a historical or abstract formulation where retract closure is not yet available, the proof of $(6a,b)\Rightarrow(6c)$ requires that retracts of $\W$-aspherical objects be $\W$-aspherical. This is weaker than asking that every arrow retract of every member of $\W$ belong to $\W$, but the latter suffices.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Proposition 3.3 and Corollary 3.7, ms. 22, 26–27; XII ms. 265–272
notes: Pointed cofibers and their cone-vertex sections are retained. The wedge comparison uses e→Z_0. Object retract closure suffices for the third clause.

statement: The formal fibration implication scheme. Let $\mathcal F$ be a class of arrows in a category with the relevant pullbacks. Define \[ \begin{array}{rcl} \mathrm A(\mathcal F)&:&\mathcal F\subseteq\Fib_{\W},\\ \mathrm B(\mathcal F)&:&\text{every }\W\text{-map over }S\text{ between }\mathcal F\text{-objects lies in }\W_S^u,\\ \mathrm C(\mathcal F)&:&\mathcal F\cap\W\subseteq\W^u. \end{array} \] If every map factors as a $\W$-map followed by a map in $\mathcal F$, then $\mathrm A(\mathcal F)\Rightarrow\mathrm B(\mathcal F)$. If identities belong to $\mathcal F$, then $\mathrm B(\mathcal F)\Rightarrow\mathrm C(\mathcal F)$. If in addition $\mathcal F$ is closed under pullback and composition and contains all terminal maps, then \[ \mathrm A(\mathcal F)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathrm B(\mathcal F)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mathrm C(\mathcal F). \] These are the precise premises of XVI Lemmas~4.4.1 and~4.4.3.
notes: Every Brown premise is stated; enough fibrations alone does not identify arbitrary weak or Grothendieck fibrations with intrinsic fibrations.

statement: Replacement transfers the weak-fibration formulations. Suppose two classes $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ have the following comparison property: each $p:X\to S$ in $\mathcal F$ factors as \[ X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{\overline p}S, \qquad j\in\W_S^u,\quad\overline p\in\mathcal G. \] Then $\mathrm A(\mathcal G)\Rightarrow\mathrm A(\mathcal F)$ and $\mathrm C(\mathcal G)\Rightarrow\mathrm C(\mathcal F)$. If the replacements are functorial over $S$ on morphisms between objects in $\mathcal F$, then also $\mathrm B(\mathcal G)\Rightarrow\mathrm B(\mathcal F)$.
notes: The B transfer requires functorial replacements over the fixed base, not merely objectwise existence.

statement: The complete list of additional arrows asserted in XVI \S4. Besides the formal implications just proved, XVI, manuscript pp.~45--70, asserts the following. For $V\subseteq\W$ one has \[ \mathrm A_V\Rightarrow\mathrm B_V\Rightarrow\mathrm C_V\Rightarrow D_V\Rightarrow(7F), \] and the same chain with $V=\W$. It asserts \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm A_\W&\Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\mathrm C_\W+\mathcal F_\W\text{ closed under composition}\bigr) \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \bigl(\mathrm C_\W+\Fib^{\mathrm{weak}}_\W\text{ closed under composition}\bigr). \end{aligned} \] It asserts $\mathrm A_V\Leftrightarrow\mathrm B_V\Leftrightarrow\mathrm C_V$ if $\mathcal F_V$ is closed under composition, in particular if $V$ satisfies Loc~(7). Its summary 4.4.13 additionally asserts that sequential-colimit closure of $V$ makes all four reference conditions equivalent; sequential-colimit closure of both $V$ and $\W$ makes all eight conditions equivalent; and strong saturation plus Loc~(3 bis) for $\W$ gives $\mathrm B_\W\Rightarrow\mathrm A_\W$. The printed summary also says that $(7F)$ for $V$ suffices to identify the first three reference conditions; its earlier argument at 4.4.6 had used the stronger condition Loc~(7).
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 45–70; 4.4.6, 4.4.13, 4.4.15, literal heading 4.16 and footnote 36
notes: Records the manuscript arrows separately from their modern verification. The summary uses 7F for V where the earlier proof used 7; A.17 resolves the modern case.

statement: The weaker historical axiom system is not identified with the modern one here. This audit does not prove that the literal historical Loc~$(1,2,3)$ with absolute Theorem~A implies relative Theorem~A, Loc~$(3\mathrm{bis})$. Consequently it does not use the modern strong-saturation theorem to settle the original eight-condition implication diagram for every class satisfying only that weaker definition. The unresolved statement here is precisely that implication between axiom systems; a first nonterminal test base is $[1]$, since the relative axiom over $e$ is tautological. The minimum $W_\omega=\Winfty$ is already settled by the distinct weak-localizer theorem in \claimref{A.19}; it is not part of this residual obligation.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Loc (3) versus Loc (3 bis); historical eight-condition implication diagram
notes: Open in this audit: absolute historical Theorem A ⇒ relative Theorem A. Test base [1] is the first nonterminal instance. Not a claim of newly open literature status; minimum itself is settled.

statement: All eight fibration variants collapse in the modern convention. Let $V\subseteq\W$ be modern fundamental localizers. Each of the eight conditions $\mathrm A_\W,\allowbreak\mathrm B_\W,\allowbreak\mathrm C_\W,\allowbreak D_\W,\allowbreak\mathrm A_V,\allowbreak\mathrm B_V,\allowbreak\mathrm C_V,\allowbreak D_V$ is equivalent to \[ \W=\Winfty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\W=\Fl(\Cat). \] No accessibility or filtered-colimit hypothesis is needed for this conclusion. Thus every conditional arrow in \claimref{A.15} is valid for the modern convention, including the summary's $(7F)$-for-$V$ formulation, although that formulation is not what the earlier manuscript proof establishes.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 45–70 and 83–85; all eight fibration formulations
notes: No accessibility hypothesis. All eight conditions imply homotopy-pullback stability, then W=W_infinity or total; cited full proof E.4–E.5.

statement: The coproduct consequences accompanying the implication diagram. Write Loc~$(4a_0)$ for preservation of finite coproducts of equivalences, Loc~$(4a)$ for preservation of all small coproducts, and Loc~$(4b)$ for reflection of equivalences by coproducts of families with a common indexing set. The assertions surrounding XVI \S3 and used in \S4 are \[ (6a)\Rightarrow(4a_0),\qquad (6a)+(8)\Rightarrow(4a),\qquad (7)\Rightarrow(4b). \] Consequently $(6a)+(7)+(8)$ implies Loc~$(4)$. In the modern convention $(4a)$ already follows from relative Theorem~A; no reverse excision is needed for any of these assertions.
notes: Includes arbitrary small indexing sets and empty summands; modern forward coproduct closure needs no extra Loc (8).

statement: The literal historical minimum is also the weak-homotopy localizer. Let $W_\omega$ denote the intersection of all classes satisfying the literal XVI Loc~$(1,2,3)$, where Loc~$(3)$ is absolute Theorem~A. Then \[ W_\omega=\Winfty. \] This equality does not require identifying every weak fundamental localizer with a modern fundamental localizer.
notes: Known separate weak-localizer theorem. Literal Loc1 cancellation implies Cisinski FS3, so the minimality theorem applies without relative Theorem A.

statement: The baseline used in this part. For the modern fundamental localizers fixed on the first page, $\Winfty\subseteq\W$, and $\W$ is strongly saturated and closed under retracts in $\Cat^{[1]}$. Neither assertion requires accessibility. Consequently a specified zigzag of weak homotopy equivalences of categories preserves $\W$-asphericity, and a commutative square whose vertical arrows are in $\Winfty$ transfers membership of its horizontal arrows in $\W$ in both directions.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Cisinski 2004 Theorem 2.2.11; XVI Loc (1 ter,3 bis)
notes: Modern relative-Theorem-A convention; no accessibility assumption.

statement: Forward gluing is automatic under relative Theorem A. Let $J$ be a small category, $F,G:J\to\Cat$ covariant functors, and $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$ a natural transformation with $\eta_j\in\W$ for every $j$. The functor $\int_J\eta:\int_JF\to\int_JG$ belongs to $\W$. In particular every modern fundamental localizer satisfies Loc (6 a), and the augmentation from the Grothendieck construction of a sieve-cover span to its union is in $\Winfty$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII W(7) forward; XVI Loc (6 a,6 B)
notes: Objectwise Grothendieck-construction comparison specified; empty diagrams included.

statement: A functorial categorical homotopy cofibre. For every functor $g:A\to B$ define $M_g$ on disjoint layers $A$ and $B$, with their original internal arrows and \[ \Hom_{M_g}(a,b)=\Hom_B(g(a),b),\qquad \Hom_{M_g}(b,a)=\varnothing. \] Composition of crossing arrows is induced by $g$ and composition in $B$. Adjoin an object $t$, with $\Hom(a,t)=\{*\}$ for every $a\in A$ and no arrows between $t$ and the $B$-layer. Call the resulting category $K(g)$. There is a functorial homotopy-pushout square of spaces \[ \begin{tikzcd} BA\arrow[r,"Bg"]\arrow[d]&BB\arrow[d]\\ *\arrow[r]&BK(g), \end{tikzcd} \] where $t$ supplies the basepoint. Thus $K(g)$ represents the unpointed homotopy cofibre, based at its cone point. A commutative square of functors induces a specified functor of these categories. If both vertical functors are in $\W$, the induced functor on $K(-)$ is in $\W$.
notes: Explicit functorial category K(g); A empty gives B coproduct e.

statement: The manuscript cylinder and the exact cofibration hypothesis. Let $\Cof_\W$ mean the functors $i:A\to B$ for which $B\amalg_A(-):A\backslash\Cat\to B\backslash\Cat$ preserves every $\W$-map. Every classical Dwyer map is in $\Cof_\W$. Every functor $g:A\to B$ has a functorial factorization $g=p_gj_g$, with $j_g$ a Dwyer map and $p_g\in\Winfty$. The ordinary pushout $e\amalg_A\operatorname{Cyl}(g)$ is a categorical homotopy cofibre of $g$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 228–234; XVI Loc (6 A,6 A')
notes: The manuscript uses products with endpoints, not pushout-products. Thomason 5.3(3) is not used.

statement: The exact reversible-cofibre criterion: Lead 1. For a modern fundamental localizer $\W$, the following conditions are equivalent: Loc (6 b); its single-square reverse implication Loc ($6'$ b); the biconditional Loc (6 C) for every $\W$-homotopy-cocartesian square; and \begin{equation}\label{eq:cofibercriterion} g\in\W\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K(g)\longrightarrow e\in\W \qquad\text{for every small-category functor }g. \end{equation} Under these conditions Loc (6 a,b,c), W(7), and W(7 bis) all hold. Accessibility is unnecessary. The implication from left to right in \eqref{eq:cofibercriterion} holds for every fundamental localizer.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Lead 1; XII ms. 265–272; XVI Loc (6 b,6'b,6 C)
notes: Full cube and single-square versions proved equivalent; specified cone basepoints and retracts included.

statement: The two-cofibre argument: Lead 2. Every modern fundamental localizer satisfying Loc (6 b), or only Loc ($6'$ b), contains $\WZ$. The conclusion does not require adding Loc (6 a) as an independent axiom.
notes: No extra forward axiom; empty and arbitrarily disconnected sources treated.

statement: The finite acyclic category, with a complete certificate. There is a finite category $A$ with $35$ objects and $159$ arrows, all identities included, for which $BA$ is connected and integrally acyclic and $\pi_1(BA)\ne1$.
notes: 35 objects, 159 arrows; integral Smith forms and nontrivial A5 quotient checked.

statement: The reverse axiom for $\Winfty$, including Dwyer cobase changes. The assertions that $\Winfty$ satisfies W(7), W(7 bis), Loc (6 b), or Loc (6 c) are false. XII Theorem 2 at ms.~78 and XVI Theorem 5.4 insofar as it includes Loc (6) are false. The reverse edge implications can fail even for a pushout along a classical Dwyer map.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII Theorem 2 ms. 78; XVI Theorem 5.4 ms. 79
notes: 37-object two-cone counterexample and actual Dwyer-cylinder counterexample.

statement: The two variances of the one-point collage. For a covariant functor $H:A\to\mathbf{Set}$, let $A_H$ be obtained by adjoining $x$ with $\Hom(x,a)=H(a)$, no arrows $a\to x$, and $\End(x)=\{\id\}$. If $E=\El_A(H)$ and $\pi:E\to A$, there is a literal isomorphism of simplicial sets \[ NA_H\cong NA\amalg_{NE}(\Delta^0*NE). \] Thus $BA_H$ is the homotopy cofibre of $B\pi$. Dually, for $H:A^{\op}\to\mathbf{Set}$, adjoining a last object $t$ with $\Hom(a,t)=H(a)$ gives the right-cone formula with $NE*\Delta^0$. Under the equivalent axioms in \claimref{B.5}, a full sieve $U\subset X$ with one complementary object $t$ and $\End_X(t)=\{\id\}$ satisfies \[ U\to X\in\W\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad U/t\to e\in\W. \]
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 85; TOTASPH A.10–A.11, B.1–B.2, F.20
notes: Both variances; one-point complement has only identity endomorphism.

statement: An explicit nontrivial acyclic group. Every small group $H$ embeds in a small acyclic group $M(H)$ of cardinality at most $\max(|H|,\aleph_0)$; for infinite $H$ equality holds. In particular $M(\mathbb Z)$ is countable, nontrivial, and acyclic. Its one-object category has no nonidentity idempotents.
notes: Mitosis independently proved; the stronger simple-group claim is unnecessary and unused.

statement: The one-object test required after CATHOT. Let $G$ be any nontrivial integrally acyclic small group, and let $\mathsf BG$ denote its one-object category. For every fundamental localizer satisfying Loc (6 b), $\mathsf BG\to e$ belongs to $\W$, although it does not induce an isomorphism on fundamental groups. Thus such a localizer cannot require $\pi_1$-isomorphisms even on one-object sources.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: After CATHOT consequence for Part C
notes: All acyclic groups killed by every reversible localizer; nontrivial pi1 retained in source.

statement: The amalgam is a homological suspension model. Let $H\hookrightarrow G$ be an injective homomorphism of small groups with $G$ integrally acyclic. The double mapping cylinder of $BG\leftarrow BH\to BG$ is a classifying space for $D=G*_HG$. Collapsing its two vertex spaces gives a specified map $BD\to\Sigma BH$ inducing an integral homology isomorphism. In particular this holds when $H$ is acyclic, but it does not require that assumption, and it does not assert a weak homotopy equivalence.
notes: Specified graph-of-spaces quotient is a homology equivalence; H need not be acyclic.

statement: The upper interval is not the reversible class. The assertion that $\WZ\subseteq\W$ suffices for Loc (6 b) is false. In particular $\W_0$ contains $\WZ$ and fails the cofiber criterion.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Part H wording; proposed upward-closed reading of Lead 3
notes: W0 contains WZ but fails reverse excision; four-object circle cofiber checked.

statement: The families and their model structures. For a $\mathcal U$-small spectrum $E$, we use the unreduced convention \[ \W_E=\{u:A\to B\mid E\wedge\Sigma^\infty(BA)_+ \longrightarrow E\wedge\Sigma^\infty(BB)_+\text{ is an equivalence}\}. \] For a unital ring $R$, not assumed commutative and including the zero ring, $\W_R$ means $\W_{HR}$. For an integer $n\geq0$, $\W_n$ consists of the functors inducing a bijection on $\pi_0$ and isomorphisms on all based $\pi_i$, $1\leq i\leq n$. These are accessible fundamental localizers. Their associated simplicial localizations have monomorphisms as cofibrations. On $\Cat$ they admit the left proper Thomason model structure, with the usual Thomason cofibrations. For $\W_n$ this structure is also right proper.
notes: Unreduced E-homology; all small spectra, including zero and nonconnective spectra; all unital rings, not assumed commutative; n >= 0. Verified Cisinski existence theorems are used.

statement: Sums, connectedness, filtered colimits, and accessibility. Each $\W_n$, $n\geq0$, and each $\W_E$ satisfies Loc~(4), (8), and (9). Each $\W_n$ satisfies Loc~(5). For $\W_E$, Loc~(5) holds exactly when $E\not\simeq0$. Thus it holds for $\W_R$ exactly when $R\neq0$.
notes: Nonzero generalized homology detects the number of components without a connectivity hypothesis on E. Empty families and empty sources included.

statement: The cofibration columns. Every $\W_E$, including $E=0$, satisfies Loc~(6 a), (6 b), and (6 c). Every $\W_n$, $n\geq0$, satisfies Loc~(6 a) and fails both Loc~(6 b) and Loc~(6 c).
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 17'; XII W(7); Loc (6 a,b,c)
notes: Spectral cofiber-sequence proof for E. Finite face-poset/suspension cubes refute 6b and 6c for every finite n >= 0; executable checks n = 0,1,2,3.

statement: A nullity obstruction valid for every nonzero spectrum. Let $E\neq0$, and let $A$ be an $E$-aspherical space. Then $A$ is nonempty and connected, and $\Hom(\pi_1(A,a),\mathbb Z)=0$ for every $a\in A$. For a free group $F$, the constant-map inclusion $BF\to\Map(A,BF)$ is an equivalence. Thus $BF$ is null with respect to every $E$-aspherical space.
notes: Free-group classifying spaces are null for every E-aspherical object when E is nonzero; no hypothesis on E's homotopy degrees.

statement: No nonzero homology localizer has enough intrinsic fibrations. For every spectrum $E\neq0$, $\W_E$ fails Loc~(7 F). In particular this holds for $\W_R$ for every nonzero unital ring $R$, with no restriction on its characteristic or torsion.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 91, 119-121; Loc (7 F) for homology
notes: Every nonzero spectrum fails 7F, using a non-surjective free-group endomorphism inducing the identity on stable suspension spectra. All nonzero unital coefficient rings included.

statement: Failure of the stronger fibration axioms. For $E\neq0$, and for every finite $n\geq0$, both Loc~(7) and the weakest Loc~(7 $D_{\Winfty}$) fail for $\W_E$ and $\W_n$. For $E=0$ all the fibration clauses hold.
notes: Explicit perfect groupoid replacement for homology; perfect model of * -> K(Z,n+1) for truncations. Failure already at the weakest reference localizer W_infinity.

statement: The complete axiom table for the named families. With the conventions of \claimref{C.1}, the following table is exact. In its $7D$ column we use the weakest version $7D_{\Winfty}$; failure there also means failure of all stronger $7D$ versions. \[ \begin{array}{c|cccccccccc} &4&5&6a&6b&6c&7&7D&7F&8&9\\\hline \W_R,\ R\ne0&+&+&+&+&+&-&-&-&+&+\\ \W_E,\ E\ne0&+&+&+&+&+&-&-&-&+&+\\ \W_n,\ 0\leq n<\infty&+&+&+&-&-&-&-&+&+&+\\ \W_0&+&+&+&-&-&-&-&+&+&+\\ \W_E,\ E=0&+&-&+&+&+&+&+&+&+&+ \end{array} \]
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Part C full ten-column table; XVI ms. 17', 91, 119-121
notes: Homology: all columns except 7,7D,7F hold for E != 0. Truncation: 6b,6c,7,7D fail, 7F holds. The zero theory is total and fails only Loc 5.

statement: An intrinsic description of $\Fib_{\W_0}$. Let $p:T\to B$ be a functor. For a component $B_j\subset B$, put $T_j=T\times_BB_j$, and for $b\in B_j$ let $T_b$ be the strict fiber. Then $p\in\Fib_{\W_0}$ if and only if both of the following conditions hold. First, $\pi_0(T_b)\to\pi_0(T_j)$ is a bijection for every $b$. Second, for every arrow $\beta:b\to b'$ and every $c\in\pi_0(T_j)$, there exists an arrow of $T$ over $\beta$ whose source, and hence target, lies in $c$. Equivalently, for every functor $X\to B$ the canonical map is a bijection \[ \pi_0(T\times_BX)\longrightarrow \pi_0(T)\times_{\pi_0(B)}\pi_0(X). \]
notes: Exact intrinsic description by connected strict fibers within each total component and existence of an arrow lift in each such component; includes empty components and endomorphisms.

statement: The $n$-equivalence fibration class. Let $n\geq0$ and $p:T\to B$ be a functor. Then $p\in\Fib_{\W_n}$ if and only if, for every $X\to B$, the canonical comparison is an equivalence in $\cS_{\leq n}$: \[ \tau_{\leq n}B(T\times_BX)\longrightarrow \tau_{\leq n}BT \mathbin{\times_{\tau_{\leq n}BB}} \tau_{\leq n}BX. \tag{C.9.1} \] The right-hand pullback is a homotopy pullback of $n$-types. In particular every $\W_n$-Thomason fibration belongs to $\Fib_{\W_n}$. This supplies a functorial factorization for (7 F) at every finite $n$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI ms. 91, 119-121; Fib_Wn and Loc (7 F)
notes: Exact canonical truncated-pullback criterion for every base change. Cisinski Proposition 6.2.3 supplies the same criterion under the verified properness hypothesis.

statement: Bounds for the homological fibration classes. For any spectrum $E$, $\Fib_{\W_E}$ contains all product projections $B\times K\to B$, all inclusions of unions of components, and the closure of these maps under composition, strict base change, and retracts. More generally it contains every functor $p$ for which $Np$ universally preserves $E$-equivalences of simplicial sets under strict pullback. An upper bound is the class $Q_E$ of functors $p:T\to B$ such that, for every $m\geq0$, every $\sigma:[m]\to B$, and every $i\in[m]$, the strict fiber inclusion \[ T_{\sigma(i)}\longrightarrow T\times_B[m] \] belongs to $\W_E$: one has $\Fib_{\W_E}\subseteq Q_E$. For every $E\neq0$ this upper inclusion is strict. Indeed $\Fib_{\W_E}$ omits the explicit three-sheeted action-groupoid covering described below, although that covering lies in $\Parf_{\Winfty}\cap Q_E$. For a fixed $p$, membership in $\Fib_{\W_E}$ can be tested on a set of bounded-cardinality $\W_E$-maps over its base, rather than on a proper class.
notes: Lower classes: products, component inclusions, closure operations and simplicial E-sharp nerves. Upper class Q_E tests every vertex of every finite ordinal; explicit three-sheeted cover makes the upper inclusion strict for every nonzero E. Exact set-sized testing criterion also supplied.

statement: The cofibration threshold at $\W_1$. Every functor is a $\W_0$-cofibration. If a fundamental localizer $\W$ contains $\W_1$, every functor injective on objects is a $\W$-cofibration. Hence Loc~(6 A) holds in this range. These facts do not license replacing the products with endpoint inclusions in XII, manuscript pp.~228--234, by pushout-products.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: TOTASPH F.25,F.28-F.30; XII ms. 228-234; Loc (6 A)
notes: All functors are W0-cofibrations. For W >= W1, all object injections are W-cofibrations and enough cofibrations follow. Endpoint-product and pushout-product operations remain distinct; see H.6 for the latter's obstruction.

statement: Minimality of integral homology: the valid part of Lead 3. The class $\WZ$ of all functors inducing integral homology isomorphisms on nerves is a fundamental localizer satisfying Loc (6 a,b,c). It is the smallest modern fundamental localizer satisfying Loc (6 b), and is strictly larger than $\Winfty$.
notes: Integral homology gives the least reversible fundamental localizer; full cube proof by chain complexes.

statement: The incompatibility of the two poles, with the connectivity correction. There is no modern fundamental localizer satisfying Loc (5), Loc ($7\mathrm D_{\Winfty}$), and Loc (6 b). If Loc (5) is omitted, the unique fundamental localizer satisfying both Loc ($7\mathrm D_{\Winfty}$) and Loc (6 b) is $\Fl(\Cat)$.
notes: No solution with Loc (5); total class is unique only after omitting Loc (5).

statement: A nontotal reversible localizer kills no sphere. If a fundamental localizer satisfies Loc (6 b) and makes any sphere $S^n$, $n\geq0$, aspherical, it is the total class. In particular no nontotal reversible localizer contains $\W_1$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: After TOTASPH sphere threshold; Parts C,H
notes: A nontotal reversible localizer kills no nonnegative-dimensional sphere.

statement: Both readings of the stability intersection: Lead 4. Let $\widetilde\W$ be the intersection of all modern fundamental localizers satisfying the stability list XVI Loc (1 ter, 2, 3 bis, 4, 6, 7, 8), with no prior inclusion in $\Winfty$ imposed. If Loc (6) includes its reverse half, then $\widetilde\W=\Fl(\Cat)$. If it means only Loc (6 a), then $\widetilde\W=\Winfty$. If the definition additionally insists, as the prose of XVI ms.~87 does, that $\widetilde\W\subseteq\Winfty$, there is no such localizer in the first reading.
notes: Unconstrained intersection versus an additional requested inclusion inside Winfty distinguished.

statement: What can and cannot retain simple homotopy information. No modern fundamental localizer on all small categories is a strict subclass of $\Winfty$. Even weakening relative Theorem A to the absolute version while retaining weak saturation and terminal asphericity does not produce such a subclass. A finer equivalence relation can instead be retained on finite CW or finite simplicial complexes by keeping elementary expansions, collapses, and the simple structures as geometric data. Such a structure is not a fundamental localizer. Merely localizing the category of all finite CW complexes and all cellular maps at simple homotopy equivalences does not retain the simple homotopy classification.
notes: Geometric simple structures survive; ordinary localization at simple maps loses the finer classification.

statement: The finite-poset observation survives without the conjecture. Let $P$ be the face poset of the boundary of a triangle, consisting of its three vertices and three edges, and let $\operatorname{sd}P$ be the poset of nonempty chains in $P$. The last-element map $\operatorname{sd}P\to P$ is in $\Winfty$ but has no inverse up to zigzags of natural transformations of functors. Thus strict categorical homotopy is finer than weak homotopy of nerves; this fact does not produce a fundamental localizer smaller than $\Winfty$.
notes: Finite posets P and sd(P); all monotone reverse maps have degree zero.

statement: The accessible localization attached to a localizer. For an accessible fundamental localizer $\W$, let $L:\cS\rightleftarrows\cS_{\W}:\iota$ be the accessible reflective localization of spaces corresponding to $\W$. A functor $u$ is in $\W$ if and only if $L(Bu)$ is an equivalence. We identify $\cS_{\W}$ with its full subcategory of local spaces. Limits of local spaces are computed in $\cS$; colimits in $\cS_{\W}$ are obtained by applying $L$ to colimits in $\cS$. In particular $*$ is local. These conventions concern the infinity-category, not just its homotopy category.
notes: No reflector is assumed for nonaccessible classes. Local limits are ambient limits, whereas local colimits are reflected ambient colimits.

statement: Enough intrinsic fibrations mean aspherical generation. For an accessible fundamental localizer $\W$, let $\W^{\mathrm{asph}}$ be the fundamental localizer generated by $\{A\to e\mid A\text{ is }\W\text{-aspherical}\}$. The following conditions are equivalent: Loc~(7 F); $\W=\W^{\mathrm{asph}}$; $\W$ is generated by a small set of maps $A\to e$; the simplicial localization of \claimref{E.1} is right proper; and the Thomason model structure on $\Cat$ for $\W$ is right proper. Thus Loc~(7 F) is a properness condition, and does not follow merely from existence of a model structure.
notes: 7F iff aspherical generation iff set nullification iff right proper simplicial/Thomason localization. Necessity of aspherical generation does not need accessibility.

statement: The precise modality and local-cartesian dictionary. For the accessible localization $L$ of \claimref{E.1}, the conditions of \claimref{E.2} are also equivalent to each of the following: $L$ is a nullification; its local spaces form a modality; $L$ is locally cartesian in the sense that \[ L(X\times_ZA)\longrightarrow LX\times_ZA \tag{E.3.1} \] is an equivalence whenever $A,Z$ are local and $X\to Z\leftarrow A$ is a diagram of spaces; and the presentable infinity-category $\cS_{\W}$ is locally cartesian closed. Here a modality means the stable orthogonal factorization system whose right maps have local homotopy fibers and whose left maps have $L$-aspherical homotopy fibers. Its left class need not equal the class of maps inverted by $L$. Nor is its right class identified with the maximal intrinsic class $\Fib_{\W}$ in $\Cat$: every terminal projection is an intrinsic fibration, whereas a terminal map is in the modality's right class exactly when its source is local.
notes: 7F iff accessible nullification iff modality iff locally cartesian reflection iff local category is LCC, specifically for reflective subcategories of spaces. Monodromy is retained in the homotopy-limit proof. Intrinsic Cat fibrations are not identified with the modality's right class.

statement: Perfect categorical models and arbitrary homotopy pullbacks. For any fundamental localizer $\W$, Loc~(7 $D_{\Winfty}$) is equivalent to stability of the induced $\W$-equivalences of spaces under arbitrary homotopy pullback. No accessibility hypothesis is needed for this equivalence. The test class $\Parf_{\Winfty}$ is essential: replacing homotopy pullbacks by arbitrary strict pullbacks of categories would be stronger and false even for $\Winfty$.
notes: Equivalence with arbitrary homotopy-pullback stability, without accessibility of W. Perfect factorization uses the accessible minimal localizer W_infinity only. Cisinski 5.3.14, 6.4.14 and 6.2.3 verify the model transfer.

statement: The fibration pole has two possibilities. For a fundamental localizer in the convention of this paper, Loc~(7 $D_{\Winfty}$) holds if and only if $\W=\Winfty$ or $\W=\Fl(\Cat)$. Therefore all eight variants $A,B,C,D,A_V,B_V,C_V,D_V$ of XVI, Section 4.4, for $\Winfty\subset V\subset\W$, are equivalent in this modern axiom system and have precisely these two solutions. Loc~(5) excludes the second solution. This strengthens the conclusion $\W\subset\Winfty$ of XVI, Theorem 6.1, by combining it with minimality.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XVI Theorem 6.1, ms. 83; section 4.4 eight variants
notes: All eight modern fibration variants have only W_infinity and the total class as solutions, even without accessibility. Loc 5 excludes the total class.

statement: Lead 5 with its exact hypotheses. For an accessible fundamental localizer, the following are equivalent: Loc~(7); Loc~(7 $D_{\Winfty}$); $L$ preserves finite limits; and $L$ is either the identity localization of spaces or the localization to the terminal infinity-category. These equivalences do not identify Loc~(7 F) with left exactness. Instead (7 F) has the strictly weaker meanings in \claimref{E.2} and \claimref{E.3}.
notes: 7 and weakest 7D are equivalent to left exactness in the accessible setting. Spaces have exactly two reflective lex localizations. Finite truncation is modal and LCC but not lex.

statement: The three classes on XII, manuscript pp.~178--187. For $n\geq2$ and a map of spaces $f:X\to Y$, use the manuscript's definitions with their missing range made explicit: $a_n$ means that every homotopy fiber is nonempty, connected, and has $\pi_i=0$ for $1\leq i\leq n$; $b_n$ means that $\tau_{\leq n}f$ is an equivalence; and $c_n$ means that \[ H^i(Y;M)\longrightarrow H^i(X;f^*M) \] is an isomorphism for $0\leq i\leq n$, for every local system of sets at $i=0$, groups at $i=1$, and abelian groups at $i\geq2$. Then $a_n$ is the left class of the $n$-truncation modality, whereas $b_n$ is its class of reflective equivalences. Precisely, \[ a_n\subset b_n\subset c_n\subset a_{n-1}, \qquad a_n=(b_n)^{\mathrm{univ}}, \] where universal means stable membership under all homotopy base changes. Moreover $b_2=c_2$, while $b_n\subsetneq c_n$ for every $n\geq3$. Thus the manuscript's expectation that all displayed implications are strict is false at $n=2$. The final suggestion on manuscript p.~187 that $a_n$ itself defines the localizer of $n$-types is also false: $a_n$ fails two out of three. That localizer is $b_n$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 178-187; footnotes 116-117; final assertion on ms. 187
notes: Full local-coefficient proof of a_n subset b_n subset c_n subset a_(n-1); b2=c2 corrects strictness. a_n is universal b_n and fails 2/3, so b_n defines W_n. Whitehead attaching maps prove strictness for n >= 3; finite cellular checks n = 3,...,8.

statement: The spectrum in the proposed assignment. For a map $f:X\to Y$ of $\mathcal U$-small spaces, put \[ C_f=Y\amalg_X^h *,\qquad D(f)=\cofib(\Sigma^\infty_+X\xrightarrow{\Sigma^\infty_+f} \Sigma^\infty_+Y)\in\Sp. \] The cone point gives $C_f$ a specified basepoint. There is a natural equivalence $D(f)\simeq\Sigma^\infty C_f$, with \emph{reduced} suspension spectrum on the right. Moreover, $D(C_f\to *)\simeq\Sigma D(f)$. Both assertions include empty and disconnected $X,Y$.
notes: Reduced suspension spectrum at the specified cone point; includes empty and disconnected cases.

statement: Localizing subcategories give reversible excision. Let $\mathcal L$ be a full replete localizing subcategory of $\Ho(\Sp_{\mathcal U})$: it is closed under all shifts, distinguished triangles, retracts, and $\mathcal U$-small coproducts. Define \[ R(\mathcal L)=\{u:A\to B\text{ in }\Cat\mid D(Bu)\in\mathcal L\}. \] Then $R(\mathcal L)$ is a strongly saturated fundamental localizer in the relative-Theorem-A convention of this paper. It satisfies Loc (6 a), Loc (6 b), and Loc (6 c), and for every functor $u$ it satisfies \[ u\in R(\mathcal L)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C_{Bu}\text{ is }R(\mathcal L)\text{-aspherical}. \] The asphericity of a space means that of any category-of-simplices model of that space; the comparison weak equivalences make the definition independent of the model.
notes: No accessibility needed for order-theoretic class; localizing kernel assumed retract closed.

statement: Accessibility and the size of the assignments. If $\mathcal L$ is generated by a $\mathcal U$-small set of spectra, then $R(\mathcal L)$ is accessible. If a fundamental localizer $\W$ is generated by a $\mathcal U$-small set $S$ of functors, then \[ T(\W):=\operatorname{loc}\{D(Bu):u\in\W\} =\operatorname{loc}\{D(Bs):s\in S\}. \] Without these set-generation hypotheses the order-theoretic assignments still exist in the larger universe; we make no assertion that the corresponding localizations are accessible in $\mathcal U$.
notes: Accessibility restricted to set-generated stable kernels; no Vopenka assumption.

statement: The Galois connection. Order fundamental localizers and full localizing subcategories of $\Ho(\Sp)$ by inclusion. With $T$ and $R$ as above, \[ T(\W)\subseteq\mathcal L \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \W\subseteq R(\mathcal L). \] Consequently $RT$ is an increasing idempotent closure operator on fundamental localizers, while $TR$ is a decreasing idempotent operator on localizing subcategories. The assignments restrict to the accessible and set-generated objects described in \claimref{F.3}.
notes: Order preserving adjunction; RT is closure, TR is interior.

statement: The exact image and the fibers of stable detection. Let $\mathscr D$ denote the class of spectra equivalent to $\Sigma^\infty K$ for a pointed $\mathcal U$-small space $K$. Then \[ TR(\mathcal L)=\operatorname{loc}(\mathcal L\cap\mathscr D). \] The stable fixed objects are exactly the localizing subcategories generated by the suspension spectra which they contain. The unstable fixed objects are exactly the localizers $\W=RT(\W)$, equivalently those of the form $R(\mathcal L)$. On these two fixed-object posets, $T$ and $R$ are inverse order isomorphisms. Furthermore, \[ R(\mathcal L)=R(\mathcal M) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal L\cap\mathscr D=\mathcal M\cap\mathscr D. \] Thus each nonempty fiber of $R$ has the least member $TR(\mathcal L)$; its other members are exactly the localizing subcategories with the same intersection with $\mathscr D$. Each such fiber is order convex.
notes: Exact formal image and fibers; does not assert every reversible localizer is RT-fixed.

statement: The zero stable subcategory detects integral homology. One has $R(0)=\WZ$. In fact \[ T(\W)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\W\subseteq\WZ. \] In particular, every fundamental localizer between $\Winfty$ and $\WZ$ has the same image $0$ under $T$, and $RT(\W)=\WZ$ throughout this interval.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Lead 6, zero localizing subcategory; Part H interval
notes: Stable integral Hurewicz detects zero connective spectra.

statement: The proposed bijection with all localizing subcategories. The assignments in Lead 6 are not inverse bijections, even with accessibility and set generation. Let \[ \mathcal L_{\mathbb Z} =\{V\in\Ho(\Sp):H\mathbb Z\wedge V=0\}. \] Then $\mathcal L_{\mathbb Z}\ne0$, but $R(\mathcal L_{\mathbb Z})=R(0)=\WZ$ and $TR(\mathcal L_{\mathbb Z})=0$.
notes: 0 versus ker(HZ smash -), or 0 versus loc(K(n)), have identical space equivalences.

statement: A homology equivalence between free-group categories. Let $F=\langle x,y\rangle$ be the free group on two generators. The one-object category $BF$ has arrows the reduced words in $x,x^{-1},y,y^{-1}$, identity the empty word, and composition concatenation followed by free reduction. The endomorphism \[ \alpha:F\longrightarrow F,\qquad \alpha(x)=x,\quad \alpha(y)=yxyx^{-1}y^{-1} \] defines a functor $B\alpha:BF\to BF$ which is an integral homology equivalence, and indeed an $E$-homology equivalence for every spectrum $E$, but is not a weak homotopy equivalence. The group $F$ has no nontrivial perfect subgroup.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Parts C,E,F: homology and nullification; XVI Loc (7 F)
notes: Code and complete output verify BS3 and the non-surjectivity certificate; also action orbits for Part C.

statement: The plus localizer has the same aspherical objects as integral homology. Let $P_+$ be nullification at the universal acyclic space of \citet[Theorem 4.3]{FBerrickCasacuberta1999}, applied componentwise to all spaces, with $P_+(\varnothing)=\varnothing$. It is the plus construction with respect to the largest perfect subgroup of each component's fundamental group. Put $\W_+=\{u:A\to B\mid P_+(Bu)\text{ is a weak equivalence}\}$. Then $\W_+$ is an accessible fundamental localizer, and \[ \Winfty\subsetneq\W_+\subsetneq\WZ. \] Its aspherical categories are precisely the nonempty connected integrally acyclic categories, hence are exactly the $\WZ$-aspherical categories. Nevertheless $\W_+$ fails Loc (6 b), and $T(\W_+)=0$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Part F plus construction; Part H interval
notes: Universal plus and integral homology have equal aspherical objects but different map classes.

statement: Nullifying an individual acyclic space does not supply reversible excision. For every connected integrally acyclic small space $A$, let $P_A$ be localization at $A\to *$, and let $\W_{P_A}$ be its class of equivalences on categories. Then \[ \Winfty\subseteq\W_{P_A}\subseteq\W_+\subsetneq\WZ, \qquad T(\W_{P_A})=0. \] Every such $\W_{P_A}$ fails Loc (6 b). These assertions include contractible $A$, for which $\W_{P_A}=\Winfty$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Part F nullification at acyclic spaces
notes: All connected integrally acyclic nullification spaces, including contractible ones.

statement: The precise direct-factor condition. The retract condition relevant to Loc (1 bis) is closure in the arrow category, not merely closure under retracts of domains or codomains. Explicitly, if $u:A\to B$ and $v:C\to D$ admit commuting squares $(i_A,i_B):u\to v$ and $(r_A,r_B):v\to u$ with $r_Ai_A=\id_A$ and $r_Bi_B=\id_B$, then $v\in\W$ must imply $u\in\W$. Under the cofiber criterion of \claimref{B.5}, this condition is equivalent to closure of the class of $\W$-aspherical categories under retracts. For stable detection, closure of $\mathcal L$ under retracts implies this condition for $R(\mathcal L)$. Conversely, retract closure of $R(\mathcal L)$ alone does not recover all spectral retract data of $\mathcal L$.
notes: Arrow-category retracts; automatic for the modern relative-Theorem-A definition by Cisinski 4.2.4.

statement: Intersection and union aspherical imply both pieces aspherical. Let $\W$ be a fundamental localizer in this paper's convention. Let $U,V\subseteq X$ be full sieves with $U\cup V=X$, and put $K=U\cap V$. If $K\to e$ and $X\to e$ belong to $\W$, then $U\to e$ and $V\to e$ belong to $\W$. Thus row XIIba-A-053 has an affirmative answer in the specified convention. Full W(7 bis), and in particular its reverse half, is unnecessary for this implication.
notes: Forward gluing plus automatic retract closure suffice; reverse excision unused.

statement: The homology examples and the distinction from arbitrary localizing kernels. For any spectrum $E$, define $\mathcal A_E=\{V:E\wedge V=0\}$. Then $R(\mathcal A_E)=\W_E$, where generalized homology of an unpointed space $X$ means $\pi_*(E\wedge\Sigma^\infty_+X)$ in all integer degrees. No ring structure on $E$ is required. Every full localizing subcategory of $\Ho(\Sp)$ is a tensor ideal. Nevertheless the definition of $R(\mathcal L)$ does not require a proof that $\mathcal L=\mathcal A_E$ for some $E$.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Part F generalized homology and arbitrary stable kernels
notes: All integer degrees, unpointed E-homology defined by adjoining a disjoint basepoint X_+; E need not be a ring.

statement: Two additional classification assertions not proved by the Galois connection. We have not established either of the following assertions in this audit. First, every accessible fundamental localizer satisfying Loc (6 b) is fixed by $RT$. Equivalently, for such a $\W$ and every functor $g$, \[ D(Bg)\in\operatorname{loc}\{D(Bu):u\in\W\} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g\in\W. \] Second, a specified arbitrary localizing subcategory of spectra need not be declared a homological Bousfield class merely because it is generated by a set. A concrete test not decided here is \[ \operatorname{loc}(H\mathbb F_p) \stackrel{?}{=}\{V:E\wedge V=0\}\quad\text{for some spectrum }E. \] We record the latter as an unresolved verification in this audit, not as a new assertion about the present research status of that particular example.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: Part F residual image converse and Bousfield representability
notes: Open means unresolved in this audit. Berger-Ratkovic stable embedding requires fully faithful suspension. The loc(HFp) question is exactly equality with the a(HFp)-acyclics; the 2026 Putzstuck retract-conjecture counterexample does not settle it.

statement: The distinction needed to classify the manuscript's uses. In the modern convention, forward homotopy-pushout invariance is available for every fundamental localizer. A statement asserting reverse cancellation for \emph{all} homotopy-pushout squares is equivalent to the conditions of \claimref{B.5}. The weaker assertion that the intersection and union of two sieves are aspherical only requires forward gluing and retract closure to imply that the pieces are aspherical. It does not imply reverse cancellation for maps of such squares.
notes: Object-level intersection/union implication is true for every modern W by forward gluing and retracts; it must not be equated with the failed map-level 6c.

statement: The global reverse claims at the start of XII \S5. XII Th\'eor\`eme~2, manuscript p.~78, and its interpretation of reverse excision as a property of ordinary $\mathrm{HOT}$ at pp.~79--80 are false. The forward clauses of W(7) and W(7 bis) hold for $\Winfty$; the reverse clauses, and the cube clause later called Loc~$(6c)$, fail. The conditional implications between those axioms at pp.~76--78 remain valid, with retract closure for the object-to-cube reduction.
notes: Finite A with 35 objects and 159 arrows, and its two cones; acyclic-group alternative also specified.

statement: Reverse cancellation remains false along genuine Dwyer maps. The reverse directions asserted conditionally in XII Proposition~6, manuscript pp.~81--83, Th\'eor\`eme~3, pp.~108--109, and footnote~124, pp.~227--228, do not hold for $\Winfty$, even when the attaching sieve is a genuine Dwyer inclusion and all the source's boundary and closure conditions hold. Their forward directions are valid. The full conditional statements are valid when the appropriate reverse axiom is assumed.
notes: Reverse cancellation fails even for a genuine Dwyer cofibration; full reverse hypotheses repair the conditional claims.

statement: The one-point-complement converse. The one-point-complement equivalence at XII, manuscript p.~85, and again Corollaries~4--5, pp.~149--151, is valid under W(7 bis), but false for $\Winfty$. So are reverse formulations in Proposition~7, pp.~84--85, when specialized to a one-point complement. Their direct implication from aspherical comma categories is valid for every fundamental localizer.
manuscript_rows_or_pages_settled: XII ms. 85, 149–151; Proposition 7 and one-point-complement tests
notes: One-point complement is required to have only the identity endomorphism; the reverse assertion is conditional on full excision.

statement: The total-asphericity gluing argument has a separate error. XII Proposition~9(b), manuscript pp.~97--98, its retraction-based repair at pp.~98--100, and its conclusion that the outgoing fork is totally aspherical are false even for $\W=\W_R$ with $R$ any nonzero commutative ring. These errors persist when full W(7) is valid. The additional retractions do not make the relevant left Kan extension preserve monomorphisms or intersections.
notes: Four objects and ten arrows give S^2; an ordinary final fork is contractible. The mono-under-right-adjoint claim about Kan extension is independently false.

statement: The suspension construction used to disprove cofibrancy survives. The counterexample mechanism of XII, manuscript pp.~104--107, survives for $\Winfty$ when its auxiliary category $Y$ is nonempty and simply connected. Its conclusion that the resulting $X'$ is weakly contractible exactly when $Y$ is weakly contractible has an independent proof. statement: A sieve and its complementary cosieve always give the proposed homotopy pushout. statement: The factorization-only hypotheses supply the required abstract finite calculus. Let $\mathcal M$ be a category, in a fixed universe large enough for the diagrams under consideration, with all pushouts. Let $\W\subseteq\Fl(\mathcal M)$ contain the isomorphisms and satisfy two out of three. Assume that every arrow factors as an intrinsic $\W$-cofibration followed by a member of $\W$. These are the pushout-dual premises of XII \S7 and the factorization premise at manuscript p.~272. They suffice for a choice-independent notion of homotopy-pushout square, with specified weak comparison maps between its models, invariance under objectwise $\W$-maps, and the compatible finite comparisons needed for the square-of-cofibres lemma at p.~268. If $\mathcal M$ has a terminal object $e$, that lemma holds for the actual cofibres of a map of homotopy-pushout squares whose four vertical maps are cofibrations. Under these same hypotheses, theorem parts~1\,$^\circ$--2\,$^\circ$ at XII pp.~272--274 are valid after correcting Cons~2 to say \emph{cocartesian}. Corollary~2 is valid with its stated conservativity and object-retract assumptions. No global initial object, cofibrancy or fibrancy of the terminal object, pushout-product axiom, or globally functorial factorization is required. The finite absolute diagrams used here have a least vertex: spans, squares, and their products. We do not assert the existence of arbitrary finite homotopy colimits in $\mathcal M$.

statement: The inclusions and the two poles. Every modern fundamental localizer contains $\Winfty$. Among those satisfying Loc (5), exactly $\Winfty$ satisfies Loc ($7D_{\Winfty}$). The localizers satisfying Loc (6 b) have least member $\WZ$, but do not form the whole upper interval above $\WZ$. There are strict inclusions \[ \Winfty\subsetneq\W_+\subsetneq\WZ\subsetneq\W_0. \] Neither $\W_+$ nor $\W_0$ satisfies Loc (6 b). For each finite $n\geq1$, $\W_n$ and $\WZ$ are incomparable. No nontotal localizer satisfying Loc (6 b) contains $\W_1$.

statement: Total asphericity and ordinary final images. For a small category $A$, define $T_\W(A)$ by requiring that \[ B/(f_!1_A)\longrightarrow e\quad\text{belong to }\W \] for every small $B$ and every functor $f:A\to B$. Here $f_!$ is ordinary left Kan extension of presheaves along $f^{\op}$, and $B/H$ is the presheaf category of elements. Then $T_\W(A)$ holds if and only if every target $B$ of an ordinary final functor $A\to B$ is $\W$-aspherical. Final means that every $b\backslash A$ is nonempty and connected; no homotopical finality is implicit.
notes: Ordinary presheaf Kan extension; finality means nonempty connected commas.

statement: The entire interval is invisible to total asphericity. For every small category $A$, \[ T_{\Winfty}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_{\WZ}(A). \] Consequently these conditions are equivalent to $T_\W(A)$ for every $\Winfty\subseteq\W\subseteq\WZ$. Their intrinsic criterion is that $A$ be nonempty and connected and that, for every covariant functor $H:A\to\mathbf{Set}$, every connected component of $\El_A(H)$ be integrally acyclic. In this criterion ``integrally acyclic'' may equivalently be replaced by ``weakly contractible''.
notes: All covariant element categories and their coverings; empty case explicit.

statement: Above the one-type localizer, totality is plain asphericity. If $\W_1\subseteq\W$, then $T_\W(A)$ is equivalent to $A\to e\in\W$ for every small $A$, including the empty category. No accessibility hypothesis is required.
notes: No accessibility; final functors give pi0 bijection and pi1 surjections.

statement: The precise boundary for all sieves to be cofibrations. For a modern fundamental localizer $\W$, the following are equivalent: $\W_1\subseteq\W$; a category of homotopy type $S^2$ is $\W$-aspherical; every object-injective functor belongs to $\Cof_\W$; and every full sieve belongs to $\Cof_\W$.
notes: Every sieve is a cofibration iff W contains W1; four-object S2 category checked.

statement: The pushout-product substitution for the manuscript's cylinders. Let $n\geq2$ and let $\Phi_n=(0\to1\leftarrow2\to\cdots\leftarrow2n)$. If $S^2$ is not $\W$-aspherical, then the pushout-product of $\{0\}\hookrightarrow[1]$ and $\{0,2n\}\hookrightarrow\Phi_n$ does not belong to $\Cof_\W$. In particular this fails for $\Winfty$ and for every nontotal localizer satisfying Loc (6 b). Moreover the only class of full-sieve $\W$-cofibrations stable under taking this pushout-product is a class consisting of isomorphisms. Products with the endpoint inclusion, as used in \claimref{B.4}, have no such defect.
notes: Uniform n>=2 coend proof, complete n=2,3 computations, and arrow-retract obstruction.

statement: Stability of the unpointed derivator. In particular none of the homology localizers for nonzero theories gives a stable unpointed derivator, although its equivalences admit the stable detection of Part F.
